title: Spot and Close IAM Escalation Paths
objective: Review four IAM policies in your own simulated account, identify which permissions let a principal raise its own privileges, and rewrite each policy so the legitimate job still works but the escalation path is closed.
successCriteria: You identified every escalation-capable permission (CreatePolicyVersion, AttachUserPolicy, UpdateAssumeRolePolicy, PassRole on *) and the principal holding it
You rewrote all four policies so each scoped job still works and the dangerous capability is denied
A re-check of the remediated policy set reports zero paths to admin
hints: Start with the risk report: which principals does it say can reach admin, and through which IAM action?
Every one of these actions is dangerous because the Resource is `*`. Ask: which exact ARNs does the job really need, and what condition pins the rest down?

Policy-version actions: scope to a team policy path and deny your own policy. AttachUserPolicy: new-hire users plus iam:PolicyARN. UpdateAssumeRolePolicy: iam:ResourceTag/tier = app. PassRole: named role ARNs plus iam:PassedToService.

resources.title: AWS docs: Security best practices in IAM (least privilege)
AWS docs: Granting a user permissions to pass a role to an AWS service
Rhino Security Labs: AWS IAM Privilege Escalation - Methods and Mitigation
PMapper (NCC Group) - IAM graph and privilege-escalation analysis

range.scenario: You are the cloud security engineer for account 111122223333. A quarterly access review flagged that several IAM policies written by different teams contain permissions that let a principal change IAM itself. Nothing has been abused: this is a pure audit of your own account. Use the audit role in the terminal to list the customer-managed policies, run the PMapper-style risk analysis, and read each flagged policy document. Work out which permissions are escalation-capable and why, rewrite the policies so each team keeps its legitimate access without the dangerous capability, then re-run the recheck helper to confirm the account is clean.

tasks.prompt: After running the risk analysis and reading the four flagged policies, which of these permissions are escalation-capable (select all that apply)?
options: iam:CreatePolicyVersion on * (DevToolingPolicy)
iam:GetPolicyVersion and iam:ListPolicyVersions on * (read-only)
iam:AttachUserPolicy on * (OnboardingPolicy)
s3:GetObject on a single reports bucket (ReportingReadPolicy)
iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy on * (RoleOpsPolicy)
tasks.explanation: CreatePolicyVersion, AttachUserPolicy and UpdateAssumeRolePolicy all let a principal change who has which permissions, so with Resource * they can be turned into administrator access. Read-only IAM calls and a scoped S3 read let you see or use data, but they do not rewrite permissions.

tasks.prompt: In the analysis report, which principal can reach admin by rewriting a policy that is attached to ITSELF? Give the user name.
tasks.explanation: user/dev-lead holds iam:CreatePolicyVersion and iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion on *, including DevToolingPolicy, which is attached to dev-lead. Publishing a more permissive default version changes the user's own permissions without anyone granting anything new. A self-referencing edge like this is exactly what graph tools highlight.

tasks.prompt: Why is iam:CreatePolicyVersion on * dangerous even though it grants no access to any data?
options: A holder can publish a new default version of a managed policy already attached to them (or a more privileged principal), replacing its permissions with broader ones
It lets the holder read every secret in Secrets Manager
It disables CloudTrail logging for the account
It deletes the account's SCPs so guardrails stop applying
tasks.explanation: A managed policy can hold up to five versions and the default version is the one that is evaluated. Whoever can create a version (or flip the default with SetDefaultPolicyVersion, including back to an old permissive version) controls what every principal attached to that policy may do. Defend by scoping the Resource to policies the team really owns and denying the principal's own policy ARN.

tasks.prompt: Fix DevToolingPolicy. dev-lead must keep read access to policies and stacks, and keep publishing/activating versions of the team's own policies under the /team-app/ path, but must NOT be able to change DevToolingPolicy itself or any other policy outside that path.

tests.name: Can publish a new version of a team-owned policy
Can activate a version of a team-owned policy
Cannot rewrite its own DevToolingPolicy
Cannot flip the default version of its own policy
Cannot touch a policy outside the team path
Can still read any policy version
Can still describe CloudFormation stacks

tasks.explanation: Two controls break the path. The Allow is limited to the /team-app/ policy path, so the permission can no longer be pointed at policies outside the team's remit. An explicit Deny on DevToolingPolicy guarantees the principal can never rewrite the policy that defines its own access, even if someone later moves it under that path.

tasks.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why the other flagged permissions are escalation-capable? (select all that apply)
options: iam:AttachUserPolicy on * lets the holder attach a powerful managed policy such as AdministratorAccess to a user they control
iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy on * lets the holder change WHO may assume a role, so a privileged role can be made assumable by the holder's own identity
iam:PassRole on * lets the holder hand any role, including an admin one, to a service that will run their code
These actions are harmless because they never read or write customer data
iam:AttachUserPolicy only works on the caller's own user, so the blast radius is small
tasks.explanation: All three are 'control-plane' permissions: they change identity relationships rather than touching data, which is exactly why they are easy to overlook. AttachUserPolicy works on any user in the account, not only the caller. The risk always depends on the target (which user, which role) and on what the policy or role being attached or passed can do.

tasks.prompt: Fix OnboardingPolicy. The HR bot must still list/get users, create users named new-hire-*, and attach ONLY the NewHireBaseline policy to those new-hire users. It must not be able to attach any other policy, nor attach anything to a non-new-hire user.

tests.name: Can create a new-hire user
Can attach NewHireBaseline to a new-hire user
Cannot attach AdministratorAccess to a new-hire user
Cannot attach even the baseline policy to an existing admin user
Cannot create users outside the new-hire naming scheme
Can still list users

tasks.explanation: Resource decides WHICH users the bot can modify, and the iam:PolicyARN condition decides WHICH policy it may attach. You need both: scoping only the user would still allow AdministratorAccess on a new hire, and scoping only the policy would allow baseline changes on privileged users. Pinning the condition key with ArnEquals is the standard guardrail for AttachUserPolicy.

tasks.prompt: Fix RoleOpsPolicy. Ops must keep read access to roles and must keep editing trust policies of ordinary application roles (tagged tier=app, names starting app-), but must NOT be able to edit the trust policy of any admin role or of a role tagged tier=admin, even if its name starts with app-.

tests.name: Can update the trust policy of an app-tier role
Cannot update the trust policy of PlatformAdminRole
Cannot update an admin-tier role that happens to be named app-*
Cannot update OrganizationAccountAccessRole
Can still read any role

tasks.explanation: Names are not a security boundary, which is why the tag condition matters: iam:ResourceTag/tier checks the tag on the target role, so a privileged role cannot hide behind an app- name. Pair the name pattern (narrow Resource) with the tag (what the role actually is). Where a team does not need the action at all, the cleaner fix is to move it to an admin-only role that is assumed with MFA.

tasks.prompt: Fix DeployerPolicy. CI must still create/update Lambda functions and register/run ECS tasks, and may pass app-lambda-exec-* roles to Lambda and app-task-* roles to ECS tasks. It must NOT be able to pass PlatformAdminRole to anything, nor pass an app role to a service it is not meant for (for example EC2).

tests.name: Can pass the Lambda exec role to Lambda
Can pass the ECS task role to ECS tasks
Cannot pass PlatformAdminRole to Lambda
Cannot pass the Lambda exec role to EC2
Can still create Lambda functions

tasks.explanation: PassRole is only as dangerous as the role being passed and the service receiving it. Listing the role ARN patterns removes the admin role from reach, and iam:PassedToService makes sure even an allowed role can only be handed to the services it was built for. This is the defensive mirror of the classic PassRole + CreateFunction escalation.

tasks.prompt: After remediating all four policies, run the recheck helper (`./recheck-iam.sh`) against the remediated policy set. It only runs once you have reviewed every flagged policy. Paste the flag from the clean report.
tasks.explanation: Verification closes the loop: a fix is not done until the same analysis that found the path no longer finds it. Re-running graph analysis after each change, and ideally in CI on every policy change, stops regressions where someone widens a policy again.

tasks.prompt: Name ONE organisation-wide guardrail type (besides the identity policies themselves) that can cap what IAM actions any team policy is able to grant, so a future over-broad policy cannot create a path to admin.
tasks.explanation: Permissions boundaries (per principal) and service control policies (per account or OU) never grant access; they set a ceiling that must also allow the action. Used together with scoped identity policies they mean a mistake in one team's policy cannot, on its own, hand out administrator access.

takeaways: Several IAM actions are privilege-escalation primitives even though they touch no data: CreatePolicyVersion/SetDefaultPolicyVersion, AttachUserPolicy, UpdateAssumeRolePolicy and PassRole. Treat each as 'can change who has what'.

The fix is almost never 'remove the permission': it is to scope Resource to the exact ARNs the job needs and add a condition (iam:PolicyARN, iam:ResourceTag, iam:PassedToService) so the permission cannot be pointed at privileged targets.
Run a graph-based analysis (PMapper, IAM Access Analyzer) regularly and gate IAM-changing permissions with permissions boundaries or SCPs so one over-broad team policy cannot become a path to admin.

title: Audit Role Trust Policies
objective: Audit the trust policies of the roles in your own simulated account, flag the ones that trust the wrong principals or lack the right conditions, and rewrite each trust policy so only the intended caller can assume it.
successCriteria: You identified the three risky roles (wildcard principal, vendor account root without ExternalId, member-account root without org condition) and ignored the safe ones
You rewrote each trust policy so only the intended role can assume it, with sts:ExternalId or aws:PrincipalOrgID where required
A re-scan of the remediated trust policies reports no external-access findings
hints: The trust policy lives in AssumeRolePolicyDocument. Read it for three things: WHO is the Principal, is it a whole account (:root) or one role, and is there a Condition?
A `:root` principal trusts every identity in that account that has sts:AssumeRole permission. Name the exact role instead, then add a condition the caller must supply.

Vendor access: Principal = the vendor's collector role + StringEquals sts:ExternalId. Internal member account: the CI role + StringEquals aws:PrincipalOrgID. Backup role: the single backup-orchestrator role in your own account.

resources.title: AWS docs: How to use an external ID when granting access to your AWS resources to a third party
AWS docs: Using IAM Access Analyzer to identify resources shared externally
AWS docs: AWS global condition context keys (aws:PrincipalOrgID)

range.scenario: You are the cloud security engineer for account 111122223333. An IAM Access Analyzer scan has raised external-access findings on IAM roles, and you need to work out which are real problems. Use the read-only audit role in the terminal to list the roles, read each trust policy and check the analyzer findings. A few roles are intentionally cross-account (a third-party analytics vendor, a CI runner in your own dev account), one is a legacy backup role nobody remembers, and some are perfectly fine. Decide which trust policies are too permissive, rewrite them so only the intended caller can assume the role, then re-run the scan helper to confirm.

tasks.prompt: Read the trust policy of every role the analyzer flagged. Which roles have a trust policy that is too permissive (select all that apply)?
options: LegacyBackupRole
PartnerAnalyticsRole
CrossAccountDeployRole
AppLambdaExecRole
SecurityAuditRole
tasks.explanation: LegacyBackupRole trusts "*", PartnerAnalyticsRole trusts a vendor account root with no ExternalId, and CrossAccountDeployRole trusts a member account root with no organisation condition. AppLambdaExecRole trusts only the Lambda service, and SecurityAuditRole trusts only its own account and demands MFA, so both are fine.

tasks.prompt: Which role is reachable by ANY AWS principal on the internet (the analyzer marks it isPublic: true)? Give the role name.
tasks.explanation: LegacyBackupRole has Principal {"AWS": "*"}, which means any authenticated AWS identity, in any account, that has (or can obtain) sts:AssumeRole permission can attempt to assume it. Public roles are usually forgotten legacy integrations; the only thing standing between the world and the role is its permissions policy.

tasks.prompt: Fix LegacyBackupRole's trust policy. Only the backup-orchestrator role in THIS account (including its sessions) may assume it. No other role in the account, and no outside principal, may.

tests.name: backup-orchestrator can assume the role
A backup-orchestrator session can assume the role
Another role in the same account cannot assume it
A random user in an unrelated account cannot assume it

tasks.explanation: The fix replaces the wildcard with the one identity that needs the role. Naming a role (not the account root) matters: a root principal would delegate the decision to every identity policy in the account, while a role ARN grants only that role. A wildcard principal in a trust policy is almost never intended.

tasks.prompt: PartnerAnalyticsRole trusts the vendor's whole account root with no condition. What is the real risk, and what does sts:ExternalId add?
options: Any identity in the vendor account with sts:AssumeRole permission, including the vendor acting on behalf of ANOTHER customer, can assume your role; the ExternalId ties the request to your tenant so it cannot be replayed for someone else
The vendor can read your S3 buckets directly without assuming anything
ExternalId encrypts the temporary credentials returned by STS
ExternalId makes the role usable only from the vendor's IP addresses
tasks.explanation: This is the confused-deputy problem. The vendor is a shared service; without a customer-unique ExternalId that the vendor must present, a second customer of the vendor could trick the service into assuming YOUR role. ExternalId is not a password or encryption: it is an identifier the vendor must include so the assume-role request is tied to your tenant. Also scope the Principal to the vendor's exact role instead of the account root.

tasks.prompt: Fix PartnerAnalyticsRole's trust policy. Only Northwind's northwind-collector role may assume it, and only when it supplies the agreed ExternalId (see integration-notes.txt). Other roles in the vendor's account, and unrelated principals, must be denied.

tests.name: northwind-collector with the correct ExternalId can assume
northwind-collector without an ExternalId is denied
northwind-collector with a wrong ExternalId is denied
Another role in the vendor's account is denied even with the ExternalId
An unrelated account's role is denied

tasks.explanation: Two independent controls: the Principal narrows trust from the vendor's entire account to the single role that should call you, and the sts:ExternalId condition (StringEquals) makes the request prove it is acting for your tenant. A missing ExternalId fails a StringEquals condition, so forgetting to send it is denied rather than ignored.

tasks.prompt: CrossAccountDeployRole trusts a member account in your own AWS Organization. Which global condition key restricts a trust policy to principals that belong to your organisation?
tasks.explanation: aws:PrincipalOrgID compares the caller's Organization id against yours, so even if the account id in a trust policy were mistyped or a member account were later moved out of the organisation, outsiders could not assume the role. It is a guardrail that survives account churn; it complements, not replaces, naming the exact role.

tasks.prompt: Fix CrossAccountDeployRole's trust policy. Only the ci-runner role in the dev-tools account may assume it, and only when the caller belongs to the organisation o-a1b2c3d4e5. Other roles in that account must be denied, as must callers outside the organisation.

tests.name: ci-runner inside the organisation can assume
ci-runner with a foreign organisation id is denied
Another role in the dev-tools account is denied
A same-named role in an outside account is denied
A caller with no organisation context is denied

tasks.explanation: Trusting an account root means every identity in that account with sts:AssumeRole permission can become the role, which is more than one CI job needs. Naming the exact role limits who, and aws:PrincipalOrgID limits where the caller may come from, giving defence in depth if the account or the role name is ever reused.

tasks.prompt: After fixing all three trust policies, run the lab's rescan helper (`./rescan-trust.sh`). It only runs after you have listed the analyzer findings and read each flagged role. Paste the flag from the clean report.
tasks.explanation: Remediation is complete only when the scanner that raised the finding no longer reports it. Note that the vendor role remains an intentional external-access path: the goal is not zero cross-account trust but zero UNCONDITIONED, over-broad trust.

tasks.prompt: Which AWS service continuously analyses resource policies and role trust policies and reports resources shared outside your account or organisation (the source of the findings you used)?
tasks.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer uses automated reasoning to find roles, buckets, keys and other resources that grant access to principals outside your zone of trust. Enable it in every region you use and route findings to a ticket queue so a new public trust policy is noticed within hours, not months.

takeaways: A trust policy is a resource policy on the role. Principal "*", or a whole account (:root) with no condition, means anyone (or anyone in that account with sts:AssumeRole) can become the role.

Third-party access needs the vendor's exact role as Principal plus sts:ExternalId (the confused-deputy defence). Access from your own other accounts should name the exact role and add aws:PrincipalOrgID.
Review trust policies continuously with IAM Access Analyzer: it is how an unconditioned, public or cross-account trust gets noticed before someone else notices it.
